meta.title: Whisper quantization WER degradation curve
meta.question: What INT quantization level produces the first statistically significant WER degradation in Whisper vs FP16 on clean speech?

pitch.one_line_answer: The first statistically significant accuracy loss appears at INT4: +4.9% word error rate on clean speech (p=0.001) for a 71% smaller model — while INT8 and INT5 are slightly better than full precision.
pitch.elevator: The received wisdom: quantizing Whisper below full precision hurts transcription accuracy, so pick the highest bit-width you can afford. This project measured the actual degradation curve on the LibriSpeech clean-speech corpus with a statistical test built to catch a real difference, not just eyeball one. It took all 2620 utterances to see the truth: a 100-sample run found nothing, the full dataset found everything. INT8 and INT5 slightly improve accuracy (-1.9% and -3.0% word error rate). The first real degradation appears at INT4 — and it is half the size everyone predicted: +4.9% for a 71% smaller model.

hypotheses.statement: Under LibriSpeech test-clean conditions, INT4-quantized Whisper large-v3 shows statistically significant WER degradation (p <= 0.05, Wilcoxon signed-rank) and >10% relative WER increase vs FP16 baseline.
Under LibriSpeech test-clean conditions, INT8-quantized Whisper large-v3 shows no statistically significant WER degradation vs FP16 (p > 0.05, Wilcoxon signed-rank), with relative WER increase < 5%.

headline.text: INT4 (4-bit): word error rate 5.61% vs 5.35% at full precision (+4.9% relative, p=0.001) — the first statistically significant degradation, at half the predicted magnitude
INT8 (8-bit): 5.25% vs 5.35% (-1.9%, p=0.048) — no degradation; a small statistically significant improvement
INT5 (5-bit): 5.19% vs 5.35% (-3.0%, p=0.001) — the best measured level on this corpus
A 100-sample run detected none of this: the full 2620-sample dataset was required for the statistical test to see effects this small

journey.title: Two hypotheses, one pipeline
journey.summary: The literature gave the falsifier a shape: INT4 degradation would have to be both statistically significant and exceed 10% relative word-error-rate increase to matter; INT8 was expected to be near-lossless. Two hypotheses fixed both sides of the curve before any measurement existed.

journey.title: The pipeline was verified before it was trusted
journey.summary: The transcription-to-word-error-rate-to-statistical-test pipeline was proven end-to-end on a small model first (E-004), so a surprising result could not be blamed on broken machinery.

journey.title: 100 samples said nothing
journey.summary: A 100-sample run across all four quantization levels found no statistically significant difference anywhere: INT4 at +4.2% looked like noise (p=0.57 — a gap this small would show up by chance more than half the time). The honest reading was 'we cannot detect degradation', not 'there is none'.

journey.title: 2620 samples found what 100 could not
journey.summary: Running the entire corpus turned every ambiguity into a result. INT8 and INT5 came out slightly better than full precision (-1.9% and -3.0%, both statistically significant) — mild quantization acting as a regularizer, exactly as the literature hinted. INT4 came out significantly worse: +4.9%, p=0.001. The cliff exists, it just sits at 4 bits and is half as tall as predicted.

lessons: Sample size decides which questions you get to ask. At 100 samples the answer was 'no significant degradation anywhere'; at 2620 the answer was a clean frontier: INT4. When a null result has practical consequences, treat the sample size as part of the claim — 'no detectable effect' and 'no effect' are different statements.

Verifying the pipeline on a small model before the expensive large-v3 run separated machinery errors from surprising results — the surprising final numbers would have been far less credible otherwise.

Predicting the direction of an effect is easier than predicting its size. The INT4 degradation arrived exactly where expected, at one half the predicted magnitude — which is still useful, because the practical question was always 'how much does 71% compression cost'.

limitations.baseline_wins: Full precision remains the accuracy reference in the strict sense, but on this corpus INT8 and INT5 beat it with statistical significance. The honest framing flipped: for clean speech, quantization down to 5 bits is not a sacrifice — it is a slightly better model in a much smaller file.
limitations.untested: Clean speech only; the noisy half of the corpus (test-other) was not run, and the literature predicts degradation appears earlier and larger there. Non-English corpora untested. One corrupted 200-sample chunk was re-run in a different session and environment.
limitations.next_level: The single most valuable next measurement is the same paired test on noisy speech, where the INT4 penalty is expected to grow — that is a new dataset, not more of this one. A 2-bit level (Q2_K) would also extend the curve downward.
limitations.structural: The quantization schemes tested are those of the whisper.cpp runtime (Q8_0, Q5_0, Q4_0), not every INT variant; results do not transfer to other runtimes. The 95% confidence interval for INT4 — the range that very likely contains the true value — is [5.21%, 6.03%], so the +4.9% penalty holds only within that band.

audience.who_is_this_for: Engineers choosing a whisper.cpp quantization level for memory-constrained deployments on clean speech — this is the measured trade-off table between size and accuracy they currently have to guess at.
audience.not_for: Anyone deploying on noisy or multilingual audio, where these numbers do not apply — this page says so explicitly rather than letting the clean-speech result overgeneralise.
